newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - Budget concerns to drag on Bunds.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - Budget concerns to drag on Bunds.

text.p: German debt will flounder in the medium term compared to U.S. Treasuries as concerns about the German budget take their toll, analysts said on Thursday.

German Finance Minister Theo Waigel will seek cabinet approval for the 1998 budget on July 11. The latest tax revenue forecast published last month indicates the government will have to contend with an extra 30 billion mark shortfall.
"I don't think Bunds will outperform the U.S. In Germany the direction of Bunds is going to be dictated by the budget negotiations," said Brain Venables, senior bond analyst at ABN AMRO Hoare Govett.
"Waigel and the German government are in a very difficult position to begin with and it will be difficult for the German authorities to come up with any real structural improvements to their budget."
Venables said difficulties over the budget would likely contribute to a narrowing of the 10-year U.S./German yield spread over the next one to two months to around 75 basis points.
At 1101 GMT the T-note/Bund gap was at 88 basis points, up from 73 at the beginning of the year but down from the 123 basis points of late April.
David Brickman, European economist at Yamaichi International in London, also said 75 basis points was a reasonable short term target for the 10-year spread.
"The trend of the U.S. outperforming Germany looks set to continue in the near term, because fiscal concerns in Europe are going to be offset by a general desire for safety, he said.
But Brickman said one caveat to that scenario was the economic outlook in the U.S.

The market has largely priced in no change in U.S. interest rates at the Federal Open Market Committee meeting on July 1-2, but any strengthening of activity in coming months would lead the U.S. market to look for a rate rise further out.
"That perversely could benefit Bunds in spread terms. So as the summer runs out you could actually see renewed spread widening on concerns of U.S. interest rate rises," he said.

Michael Derks, fixed income strategist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in London, was more optimistic about the performance of Bunds versus their U.S. counterparts, and noted the German debt had already started to do well in comparison to Treasuries.
"If you were heading up a portfolio you would be more inclined to be in Bunds than in Treasuries," he said.

"There is still potential cost of carry in the German curve and U.S. Treasuries are looking rather expensive up here. In all likelihood we will be looking at a tightening of U.S. monetary policy over the next half year," he said.
Derks said over the next two to three months the spread was likely to move back up over 100 basis points.
In Germany too interest rates have been under the spotlight. Earlier Bundesbank official Reimut Jochimsen said he did not rule out a further German rate cut but added he did not see one.

"There is nothing really new. The statement about the potential for more interest rate cuts is a little interesting but then the Bundesbank has always said if conditions dictate they will lower interest rates," said Venables. "But the point is conditions don't warrant lower rates."
The Bundesbank kept rates unchanged after their council meeting on Thursday.
